uses.source_location: p125, final numerical definition/example; p126, Proposition2(b)
uses.attributed_claim:
Bernardi's numerical argument uses a precomplete equivalence
relation $R$ on $\N$: for every partial recursive function $f$
there is a total recursive function $g$ such that
$f(n)\mathord\downarrow$ implies $f(n)\,R\,g(n)$.
For such a relation, distinct equivalence classes are recursively
inseparable; consequently the same holds for disjoint nonempty
unions of classes. The relation $\equiv_{\PA}$ on indices defined
in \eqref{eq:uniform} is one of his examples
\cite[pp.~125--126]{Bernardi}.
The argument above obtains $A,B$ from
Corollary~\ref{cor:source-conditionals} and uses finite PA-proofs to
establish $A\subseteq P_T$ and $B\subseteq N_T$.
uses.support_explanation: The source defines numerical precompleteness exactly as totalization modulo R, lists PA-provable equality of program indices, and states distinct classes recursively inseparable. The manuscript consequence for disjoint nonempty unions follows by selecting one class in each; a separator of unions would separate those classes.

uses.source_location: pp125–126, numerical example/Proposition2; p128, Theorem2
uses.attributed_claim:
Di Paola and Heller proved recursive inseparability in dominical
recursion categories in which every morphism has a section
\cite[Theorem 8.15]{DPH}. Bernardi obtained categorical inseparability
results from precomplete equivalence relations, including PA-provable
equality of partial recursive functions among his examples
\cite[pp.~125--128]{Bernardi}.
Montagna also obtained effectively inseparable pairs in his syntactic
category $S$
\cite[Remark 3.1]{Montagna}.
uses.support_explanation: The cited span contains the PA example and the categorical inseparability theorem. Theorem2 is for nonzero disjoint unions of classes in a c+-dominical recursion category; the manuscript makes a historical attribution and does not apply it to arbitrary restriction categories.

uses.source_location: §1, pp594–595, especially numbered assertions(3),(5) and discussion after them
uses.attributed_claim:
Di Paola and Heller proposed inseparability of theorems and refutable
sentences as part of a categorical formulation of incompleteness
\cite[pp.~594--595]{DPH}. Local connectedness enters Heller's existence
theorem for recursion categories \cite[Sections 8--9]{Heller}.
Di Paola and Montagna's syntactic examples led to the question of
extending that theorem beyond locally connected sources \cite{DPM}.
Lengyel proved existence theorems using faithful iteration functors
\cite{Lengyel2004,Corrections}. The present criterion concerns
inseparability in a source already equipped with a Turing morphism.
uses.support_explanation: The introduction explicitly places recursive/effective inseparability of theorem and refutable sets among the generalized incompleteness formulations and proposes a categorical development to obtain corresponding domains.

uses.attributed_claim:
Di Paola and Heller introduced dominical categories as a setting for
recursion theory \cite{DPH}. Rosolini's $P$-categories generalized this
setting \cite{RosoliniThesis,Rosolini}. Heller adopted them and defined
prodominical categories \cite[Section 5]{Heller}.
Cockett and Lack introduced restriction categories \cite{CockettLack},
and Cockett and Hofstra developed the theory of Turing categories
\cite{CockettHofstra}. We use restriction categories, with binary
restriction products in the source recursion categories. These products
give the equivalent $P$-category structure
\cite[Proposition 4.5]{CockettLackIII}.
uses.support_explanation: The opening states the new abstract recursion-theoretic program, and §2 introduces the dominical axioms. Historical attribution is accurate.

uses.source_location: Theorem8.15 p625; Definition6.2 p612; Definition7.1 p615
uses.attributed_claim:
Di Paola and Heller proved recursive inseparability in dominical
recursion categories in which every morphism has a section
\cite[Theorem 8.15]{DPH}. Bernardi obtained categorical inseparability
results from precomplete equivalence relations, including PA-provable
equality of partial recursive functions among his examples

Composition is written $gf=g\circ f$, so $f$ is applied first.
A \emph{restriction category} is a category equipped with an assignment
that sends every morphism
$f:X\rightharpoonup Y$ to a morphism
$\bar f:X\rightharpoonup X$ satisfying
\[
 f\bar f=f,\qquad
 \bar f\bar g=\bar g\bar f,\qquad
 \overline{g\bar f}=\bar g\bar f,\qquad
 \bar h f=f\overline{hf}.
\]
In the middle two equations $g:X\rightharpoonup Z$; in the last,
$h:Y\rightharpoonup Z$ \cite{CockettLack}.
The morphisms $\bar f$ are idempotent and are called
\emph{restriction idempotents}, also called domains
\cite[Section~5]{Heller}.
The morphism $f$ is \emph{total} when $\bar f=1_X$.
The total morphisms form a subcategory, denoted by
$\operatorname{Tot}(\mathcal C)$ for a restriction category $\mathcal C$.
A \emph{restriction functor} $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ between
restriction categories satisfies $F(\bar f)=\overline{F(f)}$ for every
morphism $f$. A \emph{restriction equivalence} consists of restriction
functors in both directions whose composites are naturally isomorphic
to the respective identity functors.
uses.support_explanation: Heller calls endomorphisms equal to their domains domains; domdomφ=domφ and φ=φdomφ appear in the domain calculus. Restriction-idempotent is the current Cockett–Lack terminology, accurately identified with Heller’s domains.

the \emph{inverse image} of $a$ is the restriction idempotent
$f^*a=\overline{af}$ on $X$.

\cite[Section 6]{Heller}.

we require the agreement law
\[
